name: Jade Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential. Tell me about an ordinary day at your accounting firm.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Jade, 27, and I lead the tax review team, though I still like doing a difficult return myself. I have a master’s degree and a chartered accountancy qualification. I check the figures against source records and talk junior staff through mistakes; the hardest bit is a client bringing a box of papers two days before a deadline.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you rely on at work, and how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I keep a paper checklist beside the screen and have never used an AI tool, even when colleagues offer one. I am paid below the normal rate here, have less than a month of expenses saved, and there are few similar firms nearby. I rent alone, and my sister Eva lives across town; I would rather earn my way than ask family to carry me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can imagine another quieter tax season with fewer forms to copy. I would still want to check where every figure came from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the office that software can sort receipts, but a careful accountant must still own a tax return. We have had plenty of supposedly magic systems that just move the checking elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be relieved if the work stays familiar, yet the firm still pays me less than a team lead should earn. I have less than one month of expenses in the bank and only a few firms within reach, so even a steady year feels tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep reviewing the files with my own checklist and take the same clients through tax season. This month I would cancel the extra streaming subscription and put that amount in a separate emergency account each payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel relieved about the job, but cross at myself for letting the savings get so low. My rent and the train fare do not wait for a better salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why avoid the software if it only sorts receipts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will accept a properly checked import, but I will not put a client file into a tool I do not understand. My name is on the review sheet, and I want to trace where a number came from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you seek another firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after I see a real vacancy with a higher salary. There are not enough nearby firms for me to leave on a hunch.

say: I would say **receipt sorting** can help, but a person must own the return.
I would tell colleagues I will keep a **traceable checklist** before accepting any imported figures.
think: I am relieved the work stays familiar, yet **low pay** still leaves me exposed.
I have under a month saved and **few local firms** to turn to.
do: Keep using my **review checklist** for the same client files.
Cancel one **streaming subscription** and save that amount each payday.
feel: I feel **anxious** about ordinary bills despite relief about the job.
S0.quote: My name is on the review sheet, and I want to trace where a number came from.
fieldNote: Her resistance rests on **accountability** for figures, not a claim that software cannot sort receipts.
She feels safer in familiar work, while **low savings** and limited local vacancies remain immediate threats.

steps.text: Review the same client files with her own checklist
Cancel a streaming subscription and save its cost each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That is more serious than the small receipt sorter. I would want the owner to explain the changes to our team in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team that clients still need clean records and someone who answers for mistakes. If the firm moves drafting and checking to software, it should show us the error log and tell us whose posts will go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I fear the owner will keep the client list and halve the review team. I have never used an AI tool myself, and I do not want to gamble a client file just to look quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would ask the owner Nia for a written policy on checking AI-produced returns and for paid instruction before I touch the system. If the firm starts using it, during that first year I would log every correction by client and keep reviewing by hand until I can trace the output.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the task that made me valuable is exactly what the software reaches. I am not ready to wager my rent on somebody saying it usually works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Nia in that meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the junior post we meant to fill after tax season is still funded, and who signs off a wrong return. I would rather hear a hard answer than learn from an empty desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if she offers only a webinar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the webinar on paid time and ask for a supervised example before using a live client file. I am slow to change, yes, but that is different from refusing to learn.

say: I would ask management to show the **error log** and say who signs AI-produced returns.
I would press for a clear answer about the planned **junior post**.
think: The firm may cut my **review team**, even if clients still need a signer.
I have never used AI, so I need **supervised proof** before risking a client file.
do: Request **paid instruction** and a written review policy from Nia.
Log every **client correction** once the system reaches our files.
Take a **supervised example** before handling a live return with AI.
feel: I feel **anxious** because the software reaches my main skill.
S1.quote: I would rather hear a hard answer than learn from an empty desk.
fieldNote: She wants a **written accountability chain** before accepting software on client files.
Her willingness to take a paid webinar is cautious and **conditional**, consistent with never using AI so far.

steps.text: Take paid instruction on the firm’s AI review policy
Practice on a supervised return before using AI on live files

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a very short road when the work is all at a desk. I would think first about rent and the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the firm must tell staff and clients who is legally responsible when cheap thinking software does almost all the accounts. Robots coming around 2031 will not protect a tax desk in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I would lose the team lead job or most of its pay when AGI arrives. I am twenty-seven, highly qualified, and still have less than a month saved. A title does not pay the rent after a layoff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would put any overtime pay into cash and ask Nia whether the firm will retain a human sign-off role with a stated salary. In the first year after 2028, if the role disappears, I would stay with my sister Eva for a few months while applying for any advertised accounting compliance vacancy that pays enough to cover rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, not excited. I would have two years to decide, and I do not have two months of expenses waiting for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Eva?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my sister Eva that I might need the spare room only if I lose my pay, not as a casual way to save money. I would pay her toward food from any wage I still earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI right away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a live return. I would take a supervised course if the firm paid for it, but I cannot buy an expensive program or pretend a new certificate guarantees a post.

say: I would demand a named **human signer** and a stated salary for any retained role.
I would explain that **2028** hits our tax desks before robots arrive around 2031.
think: I expect to lose the **team lead job** or a large share of its pay.
A qualification cannot cover **rent** when my savings last under a month.
do: Put any **overtime pay** into cash before 2028.
Take a **supervised AI course** if the firm pays; ask Nia about salaried sign-off work.
Stay with Eva and seek an advertised **compliance vacancy** if my pay disappears.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely layoff and barely any buffer.
S2.quote: A title does not pay the rent after a layoff.
fieldNote: She identifies a **2028 desk loss**; robots expected in 2031 offer no delay to her core work.
Her sister’s spare room is a **contingency** after lost pay, not a chosen move today.

steps.text: Deposit overtime pay into an emergency account
Stay with sister Eva if accounting salary stops
Apply for advertised compliance vacancies paying enough for rent
Take a supervised AI course if firm pays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years sounds long until you count the tax seasons. I could use each one to build a real record of client work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives the firm time to explain how it will sign accounts once AGI handles the figures. I would want an apprenticeship route for younger staff, because a machine cannot teach judgment by leaving them out of the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still suspect my current reviewing work could go in 2031. Five years might let me save a few months and learn client disputes, but I would only move on evidence of paid work, not a promise of a new industry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting in 2026 I would ask to sit in on one client dispute each month and keep an account of the cases I help resolve. I would save part of any tax-season overtime, and in the first year after 2031 I would apply for a posted compliance role only if its salary covers my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious but less cornered than with 2028. The desk is still exposed in 2031; robots arriving in 2034 do not add three years to my accounting job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would help you learn disputes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Nia to pair me with Tomas, the senior accountant who meets clients when a tax notice is challenged. If she will not give me paid time, I would keep my current role and use the professional body's free case notes at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you switch jobs before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a firm offer with enough pay and a clear duty, because there are few accounting vacancies nearby. I will not resign for a title that sounds safe but has no salary attached.

say: I would ask for a **human sign-off** plan and apprenticeships for younger staff.
I would remind colleagues that **2031** reaches account reviews before robots arrive around 2034.
think: My current **review work** might vanish despite five years of notice.
I could build **savings** and dispute experience without betting on an unpriced vacancy.
do: Shadow Tomas on **paid time** if Nia agrees; otherwise study free professional case notes.
Save part of **tax-season overtime** for a larger buffer.
Apply only for a **posted compliance role** whose salary covers bills.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though five years allows measured preparation.
S3.quote: I will not resign for a title that sounds safe but has no salary attached.
fieldNote: Her planned learning is **supervised client work**, which fits her cautious approach better than self-directed AI experiments.
The move remains **salary dependent**, and few nearby employers constrain it.

steps.text: Shadow Tomas if Nia grants paid time; otherwise study free case notes
Save part of each tax-season overtime payment
Apply for compliance posts only if salary covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would let me build savings without leaving a job on a rumour. I would still need the firm to speak plainly about its plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years lets a firm train people properly and make promises it can afford to keep. AGI on the accounts desk in 2036 is the real date for me, not the later arrival of robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be thirty-seven by then and could have a sound reserve, but I will not call any office job safe simply because it has a new name. I would rather build a reputation for explaining disputed bills and work with a firm that puts responsibility in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current team running and ask Nia each year for paid, supervised client meeting time and a wage review. If she approves the paid time, I would join those meetings and practise explaining cases; I would also bank the first part of any rise until I have six months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I would consider an advertised client representation post only with a firm contract and enough salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the end point, but a decade gives me room to get my finances in order. I can picture making a decision without first asking Eva for a spare bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pay review never comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep saving small amounts from overtime and apply only when a better paid opening is actually posted. I will not fund a speculative course with a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a trainee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell a trainee to learn how accounts are checked and how to explain an error to a person. A firm that takes away all trainee work also takes away its future reviewers.

say: I would press firms for **paid training** and written responsibility before 2036.
I would say the **2039 robots** do not postpone the shock to account reviews.
think: Ten years could build a **six-month reserve**, but no office title is guaranteed safe.
I trust **written responsibility** and actual client experience more than a fresh job name.
do: Join **supervised client meetings** on paid time if Nia approves.
Bank the first part of each **pay rise** until six months are saved.
Consider only a **contracted client role** with enough salary after 2036.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with time to avoid a desperate move.
S4.quote: A firm that takes away all trainee work also takes away its future reviewers.
fieldNote: She uses the decade for **cash discipline** and supervised client experience, without promising to adopt AI independently.
Her willingness to change employers still requires a **real contract** and sufficient salary.

steps.text: Join supervised client meetings on paid time if Nia approves
Bank pay rises until six months of expenses are saved
Consider contracted client representation roles after 2036 only with enough salary

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose the review work and the rent money together. A clear human sign-off post with a stated salary, paid supervised training, and temporary income support after a layoff would help. I would use family help only if the pay actually stopped.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who pays when an automated tax return is wrong. I want clients to know the responsible name before the firm puts a machine between us. I also want the trainees to learn on real work while there is still time.

headlineQuote: I want clients to know the responsible name before the firm puts a machine between us.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old** chartered accountant with a master’s degree who leads tax review and rents alone.
She uses a **paper checklist** and has never tried AI, though she will accept paid supervised instruction.
Her below-standard **pay**, under-one-month savings, and few nearby firms make a lost post hard to replace.
A **2028** arrival alarms her; longer warnings let her save overtime and learn client disputes without borrowing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her review job before she has enough savings to keep paying rent.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **salaried sign-off role**, paid supervised training, and temporary income support if laid off.
